purpose: Direct ablation of the 2.csv co-expression neighbourhood term in the delivered Q2 compound-factor ranking: weight 0.5 (delivered) versus weight 0.0 (plain ridge).
question: Does adding the graph-neighbourhood term produce a reliable improvement in bootstrap stability and/or held-out predictive utility, compared with a plain ridge ranking built from exactly the same samples and pipeline?

design.samples: 250 beers, 50 panel targets from 4.csv, 219 candidate compounds (231 - 12 excluded)
design.preprocessing: per-column median imputation -> arcsinh -> column standardisation; Y centred
design.descriptive_table_graph_source: full-sample 2.csv graph, same as the delivered table

predictive_check.feature_selection: top-3 per target inside the training fold only
predictive_check.reader_model: ridge on the three selected standardised features, alpha=1.0

predictive_mae.gain: MAE(no_graph) - MAE(graph), averaged over the 50 targets
predictive_mae.breadth: at least 60% of targets not worse for the graph variant

predictive_spearman.gain: rho(graph) - rho(no_graph), averaged over the 50 targets
predictive_spearman.breadth: at least 60% of targets not worse for the graph variant

stability.note: either margin counts as a stability improvement

verdict_mapping.partial_gain: exactly one of the two axes reliable

interpretation_limits: Jaccard measures similarity only; it does not establish which ranking is correct.
Predictive utility is not causal evidence.
The delivered table uses the full-sample 2.csv graph; the predictive check rebuilds the graph inside each training fold so held-out beers never inform the graph.
The existing threshold and resolution sensitivity outputs are reused as-is and are not re-run here.
No parameter is tuned to favour the graph variant; 'no_reliable_gain' is an acceptable outcome.
